description:
El equipo BirraSpace participa en la sede de San Juan para resolver el desafío Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. Fusionamos procesamiento de datos geoespaciales, arquitectura backend en Python/FastAPI e ingeniería de sistemas inteligentes para crear soluciones de alto impacto ambiental.

Buscamos compañeros apasionados con experiencia en Diseño, Comunicacion, Ciencias de la Tierra y Diseño/Frontend para potenciar nuestra solución. ¡Sumate al equipo!
summary:
Birrap — Project summary





We developed Birrap, an interactive web atlas for exploring burning activity in San Juan, Argentina. Users select a region and date range, view daily activity on a map and calendar, and download satellite detections and analysis results.

Birrap addresses the challenge of comparing MODIS and VIIRS by using a Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF) to combine NASA FIRMS observations into a shared estimate of fire radiative power. It counts active cells using the same 1.5 km grid, daily window, and energy threshold across sensor configurations.

This helps firefighters, emergency managers, and land managers identify peak periods, explore seasonal patterns, and put recent activity in historical context.
details:
What Birrap Does

Birrap is an interactive web atlas for exploring satellite-detected burning activity in San Juan, Argentina. It combines NASA FIRMS observations from MODIS and VIIRS in a daily activity calendar and an interactive map. Users select a department or the entire province, choose a date range, and run an analysis. The application downloads missing observations, estimates fire radiative power across a common grid, and updates the map and calendar as results become available. Users can download the original detections, estimated active cells, calendar summaries, maps, and comparison charts.

The project addresses a practical problem in the satellite record. MODIS provides a long history of fire detections, while VIIRS adds finer spatial detail and continuity. Differences in pixel size, detection sensitivity, and overpass timing mean that the number of reported hotspots can change when the observing instrument changes. Birrap uses a common spatial grid and a shared definition of daily activity, then lets users compare how that indicator behaves when the analysis relies on MODIS, VIIRS, or both.

How It Works – Key Technical Innovations

On-demand retrieval and processing. When a user clicks Analyze, Birrap requests missing MODIS and VIIRS records from NASA FIRMS. Each observation provides a location, acquisition time, reported fire radiative power (FRP) in megawatts, and the dimensions of the satellite pixel. The application requests records in batches of up to five days and processes the requested interval in blocks of up to 14 days. Results are added as each block finishes, so users can begin exploring the available dates while processing continues. The calendar uses local dates in San Juan, and departmental boundaries come from Argentina’s Georef/IGN data.

A shared fire activity model. Birrap uses a Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF) to estimate FRP on a 375 m grid. The model runs 12 realizations at 10-minute intervals. Each realization tracks two quantities per cell: FRP and the fraction of fuel remaining. Fuel, the time of day, and a process-noise term determine a cell’s equilibrium intensity. The forecast then moves the current intensity toward that equilibrium. A neighboring-cell heat term represents local spread, and fuel decreases as the cell accumulates radiated energy. The variation across the 12 realizations gives the filter information about which parts of the forecast may need correction when new observations arrive.

Sensor-specific observation footprints. Birrap projects the same estimated FRP field into the geometry of each sensor. For ensemble member j and satellite pixel p, the modeled measurement is ŷⱼₚ = Σᵢ Hₚᵢ × xⱼᵢ, where xⱼᵢ is the FRP of grid cell i and Hₚᵢ is that cell’s contribution to the observation. The weight is approximated by sampling 16 points within each cell and evaluating the instrument’s spatial response there. The implementation uses a triangular response along the MODIS scan direction and a rectangular response for VIIRS. That means a broad MODIS footprint can constrain the combined power of several cells, while a smaller VIIRS footprint can provide a more localized constraint on the same field.

Local Kalman update. The filter compares modeled and measured FRP in logarithmic space. Its innovation is the logarithm of the reported FRP, with a small positive offset, minus the ensemble mean of the corresponding modeled log-FRP. Observations are weighted by distance and error variance, with local weight ρₚᵢ / Rₚ. Here, ρₚᵢ is a Gaspari–Cohn localization weight and Rₚ is the modeled error variance for the observation. The filter uses these weights to update both the local ensemble mean and its spread. When an observed detection is stronger than the ensemble can explain, the model can initialize activity inside the observed footprint before applying the update. The published prototype uses a multiplicative sensor bias factor of 1, with instrument differences represented through the observation footprints and assigned errors.

From FRP to a calendar value. Birrap averages FRP across the ensemble and integrates that average over the day. The contribution is included only when the cell lies within 6 km of a detection assimilated within the last 12 hours. The app sums the resulting energy into 1.5 km reference cells. In compact form, E = Σ(FRP × Δt) over the supported grid cells and time steps, with Δt = 1/6 hour. Each reference cell contributes one unit to the daily calendar if its estimated energy reaches the default threshold of 1 MWh. Monthly and annual summaries add these daily counts, so a cell active on three days contributes three cell-days. The map and download interface display the selected threshold and provide access to the underlying satellite detections.

Three runs for an interpretable comparison. Birrap can display MODIS-only, VIIRS-only, and combined analyses. Each uses the same calendar grid and activity threshold. This gives users a way to test how the result changes when a sensor is unavailable and to inspect where the two single-sensor estimates agree. The app also includes an archived view with detection counts at 50 km resolution and a separate monthly anomaly classification. The archived values and the LETKF activity estimates remain identifiable by their method and spatial scale.

Tools and implementation. We developed the model and data-processing pipeline in Python with NumPy and SciPy. The interface uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas. A server-side Worker retrieves observations from FIRMS, and Pyodide runs the Python model in a browser Web Worker so users can continue interacting with the page during a calculation. The prototype uses existing satellite observations and runs on standard computers.

Benefits and Goals

Birrap is intended for firefighters, emergency managers, researchers, and land managers who want to understand where and when burning activity has been concentrated. A user can select a department, identify its most active days, inspect the thermal detections behind those days, and export the results for further analysis. The provincial view supports broader seasonal comparisons, while the department and pixel views help users investigate specific episodes.

The longer-term goal is to build a daily record that remains interpretable as satellite coverage changes. Users could use such a record to compare a current episode with earlier seasons, identify unusually active periods, or guide retrospective monitoring and preparedness. Birrap distinguishes a reported satellite detection from a model estimate and identifies dates with unavailable data. That distinction matters because gaps in the detection archive can reflect cloud cover, missing overpasses, or limited sensor sensitivity.

Presenting Results

Historical retrieval case study — August 27, 2024. We used the published application’s data endpoint to request archived MODIS and VIIRS observations from NASA FIRMS. The LETKF test processed 42 detections within San Juan for the selected day. This verified that the system could retrieve records for a historical date and use them as input to generate an estimated activity field.

Recent pilot — November 8–15, 2026. The prototype included 102 FIRMS detection records within San Juan over the pilot period, with November 15 marked as partial. Using a 1.5 km reference grid and a 1 MWh threshold, the combined analysis produced 286 estimated active cell-days. The highest daily value was 80 active cells on November 11. For that same day, the MODIS-only run produced 16 active cells, while the VIIRS-only run produced 48. The combined run assimilates both streams into one evolving state, so its result can differ from both individual runs and from the sum of their daily counts.

Spatial agreement and interpretation. Across the pilot, the MODIS-only and VIIRS-only runs shared 0 of the 243 cell-days classified as active by at least one run. Spatial agreement was measured using the Jaccard index, calculated as shared active cells / active cells in either run for each day. The observations came from different overpass times, and the CSV data did not establish where both instruments had valid coverage. The comparison therefore documents disagreement under the available observations. It leaves open how much of that disagreement comes from the instruments, the timing of their passes, or changes in activity between observations.

Sensitivity analysis and visualization. The project exports a comparison across four spatial grid sizes (375 m, 1.5 km, 3 km, and 6 km) and four energy thresholds (0.5, 1, 5, and 10 MWh). This makes it possible to examine how the number of active cells and the spatial overlap respond to the chosen definition of activity. Our main results view places the MODIS-only, VIIRS-only, and combined daily counts side by side. Users can select a day on the calendar, compare the corresponding maps, and zoom in to inspect the contributing satellite records.

Technical Roadmap

Validate the comparison under matched observation conditions. The next step is to incorporate Level 2 observation masks and identify passes with comparable time windows and valid coverage. This would help distinguish unobserved cells from cells that were observed without a detection. We would then compare the two sensor configurations on dates reserved for validation and measure whether they preserve seasonal peaks, unusually active periods, and the ranking of years.

Test the stability of the historical record. The current prototype can run LETKF for requested dates with available FIRMS observations. A continuous historical production run would also need to document sensor availability, account for changes in overpass coverage, and evaluate sensitivity to grid size, threshold, and block initialization. Those tests would determine which settings are appropriate for comparing the historical MODIS era with periods that also include VIIRS.

Make results easier to reuse. The current CSV and PNG exports allow users to take their analysis outside the atlas. A future version could publish precomputed regional calendars alongside their source dates, quality flags, and processing settings. That would make recurring comparisons faster and allow other teams to reproduce the same indicators.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

We used ChatGPT to support brainstorming, code development and debugging, and the preparation of the written submission. The activity estimates are produced by the implemented Python and LETKF workflow using NASA FIRMS records. The numerical results reported here come from project runs and comparison outputs.
